phonemes.desc: Voiced bilabial nasal [m], as in English 'might'; Old Norse initial m is unchanged.
Short open back unrounded [ɑ], held brief — Old Norse short a, never the long á.

The medial g is the voiced velar fricative [ɣ] of Old Norse — softer than the English stop — followed by dental nasal [n] and short close [i]. The name ends in the ja-stem ending -i: there is no nominative -r as in Þórr or Baldr.

pronunciation.approximation: 'MAHG-ni' — a short open 'ah', the g softened to a voiced fricative between the vowels; Modern Icelandic hardens the same g to [k]: 'MAHK-ni'.

kin.label: Old Norse
kin.form: Magni, 'the strong one', son of Þórr and the giantess Járnsaxa; from the common noun magn/megn, 'strength, might'.

kin.label: Modern Icelandic
kin.form: Magni — unchanged in spelling for a thousand years and still a living given name.

kin.label: Proto-Germanic
kin.form: *maginą, 'strength, power' — the same root as Old English mægen ('main, might') and the verb magan 'be able' that gives English may and might.

kin.label: Younger Futhark
kin.form: ᛘᛅᚴᚾᛁ (m-a-k-n-i) — the ᚴ k-rune writes g, and there is no final nominative -r to carve.

pronunciation.note: Magni is Tier 2 by the mechanical rule: the normalized Old Norse form is already plain ASCII — no diacritic, no thorn, no eth for the restoration to recover. The strongest boy in the Edda has one of its plainest names; only the capital distinguishes the temple form from the input.

domains.title: Strength, Son of Thor
domains.subtitle: The Three-Night-Old Who Lifted Hrungnir's Leg — and the Heir of Mjǫllnir
domains.lead: Magni is Þórr's son by the giantess Járnsaxa: the prodigy of the Edda, three nights old when he freed his father from under the fallen Hrungnir's leg — the feat all the Æsir together could not manage. And Vafþrúðnismál looks past the end of the world to give him the hammer itself: after Ragnarǫk, Magni and his brother Móði inherit Mjǫllnir.

cards.name: Hrungnir's Leg
cards.desc: The stone giant fell with his leg across Þórr's neck, and all the Æsir could not move it. Magni, three nights old, flung it off.

cards.name: Gullfaxi
cards.desc: Gold-mane, Hrungnir's horse and the prize of the duel — Þórr gave him to the boy, and Óðinn reproved the gift.

cards.name: Mjǫllnir
cards.desc: The hammer the brothers inherit: 'Móði and Magni shall have Mjǫllnir when Vingnir's fighting is done' (Vafþrúðnismál 51).

cards.name: Járnsaxa
cards.desc: 'Iron-knife', the giantess mother — the Edda names her once, as the reason Óðinn grudged the boy his horse.

symbols.name: Hrungnir's stone leg
symbols.meaning: The weight of the giant world on the gods — and the proof that strength answers to youth, not seniority

symbols.name: Gullfaxi, the gold-maned
symbols.meaning: The horse given to the giantess's son: a father's pride against a grandfather's protocol

symbols.name: Mjǫllnir inherited
symbols.meaning: The hammer carried past Ragnarǫk — the one treasure of the old world guaranteed to the new

symbols.name: The whetstone shard
symbols.meaning: Hrungnir's broken weapon lodged in Þórr's head — the scar the duel left when the leg was lifted

mythology.lead: Magni's dossier is two scenes and a promise: a duel's aftermath, a gift reproved, and a prophecy at the end of the world. The sources tell them in a few lines each, and those lines have carried him for eight hundred years.

myths.title: The Duel at Grjótúnagarðar
myths.text: Hrungnir, the stone-hearted giant, rode his gold-maned stallion Gullfaxi into Ásgarðr on the heels of Óðinn's wager over whose horse was fastest; feasted, he drank Þórr's ale and boasted he would carry off Valhǫll and kill every god but Freyja and Sif. Þórr was summoned, and the duel was set at Grjótúnagarðar, the stone courts. The giants, fearing for Hrungnir, built him a companion of clay nine leagues tall — Mǫkkurkálfi, Mist-calf, with a mare's heart that failed him — and Hrungnir came with a heart, a shield, and a weapon all of stone, his whetstone raised. Þjálfi ran ahead and cried that Þórr would come up from below, so the giant stood on his shield to guard his feet; the thunderer came in fury and hurled Mjǫllnir through the whetstone, shattering it — one shard lodged in Þórr's own head — and Hrungnir crashed forward with his leg across Þórr's neck.

myths.title: Three Nights Old
myths.text: Þjálfi dispatched the clay giant, then went to lift Hrungnir's leg off Þórr and could not; all the Æsir came, and none of them could move it either. Then Magni arrived — the son of Þórr and the giantess Járnsaxa, and he was three nights old — and he flung the leg off his father and said it was a shame he had not come sooner: he thought he could have struck the giant dead with his bare fist. Þórr, delighted, gave him the horse Gullfaxi that Hrungnir had ridden. Óðinn objected: Þórr did wrong, he said, to give so fine a horse to the son of a giantess and not to his own father. It is the whole of Magni's boyhood in one scene — and the only childhood the Edda gives any of the gods.

myths.title: The Hammer After
myths.text: In the wisdom-contest, when Óðinn has wrung the fates of the gods from the giant Vafþrúðnir, one answer carries the brothers past the end of the world: 'Móði and Magni shall have Mjöllnir when Vingnir's fighting is done.' Vingnir is Þórr's own name. The prophecy does not flinch from what it costs — the father falls — and it does not waste words on grief: it states the inheritance, the weapon passing whole into the hands of the sons.

myths.title: The Sons at Íðavöllr
myths.text: At Ragnarǫk Þórr meets Jǫrmungandr, the Midgard serpent, and strikes it dead — and walks nine paces before he falls to the venom it spat at him. But the world does not end there. Snorri's vision of the green earth after the fire gathers the survivors at Íðavöllr, where Ásgarðr stood: Baldr and Höðr return from Hel, reconciled, and 'Þórr's sons Móði and Magni shall come there, and they shall have Mjöllnir.' The hammer survives the god. The Edda's strangest consolation is also its plainest: the fathers die in the fire, and the sons carry their tools out of it.

myths.title: The Father's Boast
myths.text: The Poetic Edda's other notice of Magni is a single genealogical line, and a revealing one. In Hárbarðsljóð, trading insults with the disguised ferryman, Þórr finally names himself at full strength: 'I am Óðinn's son, Meili's brother, and Magni's father' — Magna faðir. Of all the titles the thunderer could have chosen to close a flyting — breaker of giants, lord of Thrúðheimr, wielder of the hammer — the name he reaches for is his son's.

lore.syncretism: Magni's scene belongs to one of the oldest hero-patterns in the Indo-European world: the prodigious infant. Greek tradition sets it at the beginning of Heraklês' life — the baby strangling the serpents in his cradle, sung by Pindar in the first Nemean ode and told by Apollodorus (Library 2.4.8) — and Irish tradition builds the boyhood deeds of Cú Chulainn on the same armature, the macgnímrada of the Táin, where a child performs the feats of grown champions. The North compressed the whole pattern into a single sentence: three nights old, and already the strongest person in the story. The comparison is one of motif, not borrowing — Simek and Lindow treat Magni as a native figure of the Þórr-complex, and no line of transmission is needed. His name, meanwhile, is ordinary Germanic vocabulary: *maginą, 'strength', an element that built personal names all over the North — so that the strongest boy in the Edda wears the plainest possible label: 'the strong one'.
lore.culturalLegacy: Magni's afterlife ran quiet for centuries: the Icelandic given name Magni never died out, and Victorian mythographies kept the Hrungnir duel in circulation as one of Þórr's set-pieces — the Kearys' Heroes of Asgard (1857) retold it for generations of children. The twenty-first century put the brothers back on stage. Marvel Comics introduced Magni Thorson, a future son of Thor, in the 'Reigning' storyline of Thor in the early 2000s; and Santa Monica Studio's God of War (2018) cast Magni and Modi as their father's enforcers, carrying the pair to an audience far larger than the Edda's. Modern Heathenry keeps him among the sons of the Æsir honored for the survival of the world after Ragnarǫk — the generation for whom the hammer is kept.
lore.extendedMeditation: Magni is the Edda's answer to the question every parent eventually asks: will anyone be strong enough when I cannot stand up? The myth answers it twice. Once at Grjótúnagarðar, where the whole company of the gods heaves at a dead giant's leg and fails, and a three-night-old boy walks up and does it — strength, the story insists, is not a function of age or rank, and help can arrive from the person everyone overlooked. And once at the end of the world, where the father kills the serpent, walks nine paces, and falls — and the hammer is not buried with him. Móði and Magni carry Mjǫllnir into the green world. The Edda does not promise that the strong live forever. It promises that strength, like the hammer, is inheritable.
lore.originalScriptNote: The normalized Old Norse form is Magni — already plain ASCII, with no diacritic or distinctive letter for the restoration to recover; in the Younger Futhark the name would have been carved ᛘᛅᚴᚾᛁ (m-a-k-n-i, the ᚴ rune writing g; the name ends in the ja-stem -i, so there is no nominative -r as there is in Baldr's ᛒᛅᛚᛏᛦ). Because the name is pure ASCII, its domain was registered long ago in the ordinary way: magni.com is held by a third party outside the PuniCodex collection and is watched for release — no form of the name is currently owned, and this temple claims none.

sources.name: Poetic Edda: Vafþrúðnismál 51 ('Móði and Magni shall have Mjöllnir'), Hárbarðsljóð 53 (Þórr as 'Magni's father'), Vǫluspá 56 (Þórr's death)
Snorri Sturluson, Prose Edda: Skáldskaparmál 17 (the Hrungnir duel; Magni, three nights old, lifts the leg; Gullfaxi) and Gylfaginning 51, 53 (Þórr's fall; the sons inherit Mjöllnir at Íðavöllr)

lore.archaeology: Magni is a purely textual figure: no runestone invokes him as a god, no votive deposit or place-name can be securely tied to his cult, and no picture stone has been convincingly read as the lifting of Hrungnir's leg. The material record keeps only his name's raw material: Magni occurs as an ordinary human personal name in Viking-Age runic inscriptions (collected in Peterson's Nordiskt runnamnslexikon), built on the same magn 'strength' element that names the god. The textual witnesses hang by the usual thin threads: Vafþrúðnismál, Hárbarðsljóð, and Vǫluspá in the Codex Regius (c. 1270); Skáldskaparmál in the Codex Regius of the Prose Edda and its sister manuscripts; and the giantess þulur of the Skáldskaparmál, which list his mother Járnsaxa among the troll-women.
